analyticCertificate: Positivity follows from x(t)=x(0) exp(-integral z), and the nonnegative z boundary points inward. The normalized ratio w is well-defined for finite time. The barrier calculation gives w<=2, hence bounded x,y and no finite escape. If x tends to ell>0, the stable scalar linear z equation converges to ell^(2m)/(1-2ell^2)>0, contradicting the positive limit for x. With x->0 and bounded w, the remainder in w prime=1-w+remainder tends to zero; the exponential convolution tends to zero by splitting its integral at a fixed large time. Cesaro integration of the inverse-power derivative gives the displayed limit.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Subtract the fast nullcline and normalize its deviation: }z=y-x^2,\qquad w=z/x^{4}.
x\prime=-xz,\quad z\prime=-(1-2x^2)z+x^{4},\quad w\prime=1-w+2x^2w+4x^{4}w^2.

\textnormal{Initially the deviation is zero. Its derivative at zero is positive, so the deviation stays nonnegative and the positive first coordinate decreases. At the upper ratio barrier, }w=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad w\prime\le-1+\frac14+\frac{1}{16}<0.
0<x(t)\le\frac14,\quad0\le w(t)\le2.

\textnormal{These bounds give a global solution. If the decreasing first coordinate had a positive limit, the stable linear equation for the deviation would give a positive limiting deviation, forcing the first coordinate to decrease to zero. Thus the limit is zero.}
x(t)\to0,\qquad w\prime=1-w+o(1).
\textnormal{Variation of constants for this last scalar equation gives a ratio limit of one. Therefore }\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}x^{-4}=4w(t)\longrightarrow4.
\textnormal{Integrate and divide by time to obtain the requested normalized limit.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The polynomial is a monic generalized Laguerre polynomial. Rodrigues integration by parts shows orthogonality against every polynomial of degree below its degree for the positive weight }t^{\frac{1}{2}n}e^{-t}\quad(t>0).

\textnormal{All roots are positive and simple: otherwise the product of the positive sign-changing factors would have lower degree and its weighted inner product with the polynomial would have one strict sign, contradicting orthogonality.}
F_n(z)=\frac{P_n\prime(nz)}{P_n(nz)}=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{z-r_{n,j}/n}\quad(z<0).
zF_n(z)^2+\left(\frac{1}{2}-z+\frac1n\right)F_n(z)+1+\frac znF_n\prime(z)=0.
\textnormal{At the fixed negative argument, positive roots give uniform bounds }-1\le F_n(-1)<0,\qquad |F_n\prime(-1)|\le1.
\textnormal{Every convergent subsequence must therefore approach the unique nonnegative root of this quadratic. Compactness then gives convergence of the entire sequence.}

analyticCertificate: Rodrigues formula is proportional to t^(-alpha)e^t times the nth derivative of e^(-t)t^(n+alpha), with alpha=cn>0. Integrating against t^j for j<n transfers all n derivatives and gives zero; boundary terms vanish at both endpoints. At z=-1 each resolvent term has magnitude at most one and each derivative term at most one, giving the explicit uniform error bound. The negative algebraic root is excluded by S_n>=0; uniqueness on [0,1] plus compactness proves the limit.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The polynomial is a monic generalized Laguerre polynomial. Rodrigues integration by parts shows orthogonality against every polynomial of degree below its degree for the positive weight }t^{\frac{3}{2}n}e^{-t}\quad(t>0).

\textnormal{All roots are positive and simple: otherwise the product of the positive sign-changing factors would have lower degree and its weighted inner product with the polynomial would have one strict sign, contradicting orthogonality.}
F_n(z)=\frac{P_n\prime(nz)}{P_n(nz)}=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{z-r_{n,j}/n}\quad(z<0).
zF_n(z)^2+\left(\frac{3}{2}-z+\frac1n\right)F_n(z)+1+\frac znF_n\prime(z)=0.
\textnormal{At the fixed negative argument, positive roots give uniform bounds }-1\le F_n(-1)<0,\qquad |F_n\prime(-1)|\le1.
\textnormal{Every convergent subsequence must therefore approach the unique nonnegative root of this quadratic. Compactness then gives convergence of the entire sequence.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The polynomial is a monic generalized Laguerre polynomial. Rodrigues integration by parts shows orthogonality against every polynomial of degree below its degree for the positive weight }t^{\frac{5}{2}n}e^{-t}\quad(t>0).

\textnormal{All roots are positive and simple: otherwise the product of the positive sign-changing factors would have lower degree and its weighted inner product with the polynomial would have one strict sign, contradicting orthogonality.}
F_n(z)=\frac{P_n\prime(nz)}{P_n(nz)}=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{z-r_{n,j}/n}\quad(z<0).
zF_n(z)^2+\left(\frac{5}{2}-z+\frac1n\right)F_n(z)+1+\frac znF_n\prime(z)=0.
\textnormal{At the fixed negative argument, positive roots give uniform bounds }-1\le F_n(-1)<0,\qquad |F_n\prime(-1)|\le1.
\textnormal{Every convergent subsequence must therefore approach the unique nonnegative root of this quadratic. Compactness then gives convergence of the entire sequence.}

analyticCertificate: Rodrigues formula is proportional to t^(-alpha)e^t times the nth derivative of e^(-t)t^(n+alpha), with alpha=cn>0. Integrating against t^j for j<n transfers all n derivatives and gives zero; boundary terms vanish at both endpoints. The standard sign-change polynomial argument then proves n distinct positive roots. At z=-1 each resolvent term has magnitude at most one and each derivative term at most one, giving the explicit uniform error bound. The negative algebraic root is excluded by S_n>=0; uniqueness on [0,1] plus compactness proves the limit.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The polynomial is a monic generalized Laguerre polynomial. Rodrigues integration by parts shows orthogonality against every polynomial of degree below its degree for the positive weight }t^{4n}e^{-t}\quad(t>0).

\textnormal{All roots are positive and simple: otherwise the product of the positive sign-changing factors would have lower degree and its weighted inner product with the polynomial would have one strict sign, contradicting orthogonality.}
F_n(z)=\frac{P_n\prime(nz)}{P_n(nz)}=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{z-r_{n,j}/n}\quad(z<0).
zF_n(z)^2+\left(4-z+\frac1n\right)F_n(z)+1+\frac znF_n\prime(z)=0.
\textnormal{At the fixed negative argument, positive roots give uniform bounds }-1\le F_n(-1)<0,\qquad |F_n\prime(-1)|\le1.
\textnormal{Every convergent subsequence must therefore approach the unique nonnegative root of this quadratic. Compactness then gives convergence of the entire sequence.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The polynomial is a monic generalized Laguerre polynomial. Rodrigues integration by parts shows orthogonality against every polynomial of degree below its degree for the positive weight }t^{5n}e^{-t}\quad(t>0).

\textnormal{All roots are positive and simple: otherwise the product of the positive sign-changing factors would have lower degree and its weighted inner product with the polynomial would have one strict sign, contradicting orthogonality.}
F_n(z)=\frac{P_n\prime(nz)}{P_n(nz)}=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{z-r_{n,j}/n}\quad(z<0).
zF_n(z)^2+\left(5-z+\frac1n\right)F_n(z)+1+\frac znF_n\prime(z)=0.
\textnormal{At the fixed negative argument, positive roots give uniform bounds }-1\le F_n(-1)<0,\qquad |F_n\prime(-1)|\le1.
\textnormal{Every convergent subsequence must therefore approach the unique nonnegative root of this quadratic. Compactness then gives convergence of the entire sequence.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Zero energy for the unperturbed equation gives the positive homoclinic orbit }x_h(t)=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t,\quad v_h(t)=-\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t\tanh t,\quad\operatorname{sech}t=1/\cosh t.
\textnormal{For the dissipative part, substitute }u=\tanh t.\quad D=\int_{-1}^{1}2u^2\left[1+2^{1}(1-u^2)^{1}\right]\,\mathrm du=\frac{12}{5}.

\textnormal{The Fourier transform follows by setting }v=e^{2t}\textnormal{ in the exponential transform of the hyperbolic secant and evaluating the beta integral: }\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}t\cos t\,\mathrm dt=\frac\pi{\cosh(\pi/2)}.
\textnormal{Oddness removes the cosine-phase contribution of the velocity. Integration by parts supplies the sine-phase term.}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)\sin t\,\mathrm dt=-\frac{\sqrt2\pi}{\cosh(\pi/2)},\qquad M_A(\phi)=-\frac{12}{5}+\frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{\cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}A\sin\phi.
\textnormal{There are simple zeros precisely when the oscillating amplitude exceeds the positive dissipative constant. At equality the zero is tangent, but equality is still the infimum.}
\frac{6 \sqrt{2} \cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}{5 \pi}

analyticCertificate: The nonnegative energy derivative gives a global bounded solution. The inequality r prime>=-epsilon*r^(2m+1) keeps r uniformly bounded away from zero for 0<=epsilon*t<=1. The amplitude/phase fields and their derivatives are therefore uniformly bounded on a fixed compact annulus. F minus its mean has a bounded smooth periodic primitive G. Differentiating the near-identity correction in original time gives -epsilon*mean(F)*r^(2m+1)+O(epsilon squared), since theta prime=1+O(epsilon) and r prime=O(epsilon). Dividing by epsilon and replacing r by the corrected radius costs only O(epsilon). The scalar averaged field is Lipschitz on the compact range; Gronwall gives an O(epsilon) error uniformly on the complete slow interval. Thus the growing observation time is covered, rather than justified by a formal pointwise average.

solutionSteps: x=r\cos\theta,\quad x\prime=-r\sin\theta,\quad r(0)=1,\quad\theta(0)=0.
r\prime=-\varepsilon r^{3}F(\theta),\quad F(\theta)=\cos^{2}\theta\sin^2\theta,
\theta\prime=1-\varepsilon r^{2}\cos^{3}\theta\sin\theta.
\textnormal{On slow times between zero and one, energy dissipation and the elementary differential inequality give }(1+2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\le r\le1.
\overline F=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}F(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{(2m)!}{2\cdot4^m m!(m+1)!}\Bigg|_{m=1}=\frac{1}{8}.
\textnormal{Choose a bounded periodic primitive of the mean-zero part and correct the amplitude: }G\prime(\theta)=F(\theta)-\overline F,\quad\widetilde r=r+\varepsilon r^{3}G(\theta).

\textnormal{Direct differentiation cancels the oscillating drift. With slow time }\tau=\varepsilon t\textnormal{, the corrected variable satisfies uniformly }\frac{\mathrm d\widetilde r}{\mathrm d\tau}=-\frac{1}{8}\widetilde r^{3}+O(\varepsilon),\quad0\le\tau\le1.
\textnormal{Gronwall comparison gives uniform convergence to the averaged solution }R(\tau)=\left(1+\frac{1}{4}\tau\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}.
\textnormal{Evaluate at slow time one.}
\frac{2 \sqrt{5}}{5}

analyticCertificate: The nonnegative energy derivative gives a global bounded solution. The inequality r prime>=-epsilon*r^(2m+1) keeps r uniformly bounded away from zero for 0<=epsilon*t<=1. The amplitude/phase fields and their derivatives are therefore uniformly bounded on a fixed compact annulus. F minus its mean has a bounded smooth periodic primitive G. Differentiating the near-identity correction in original time gives -epsilon*mean(F)*r^(2m+1)+O(epsilon squared), since theta prime=1+O(epsilon) and r prime=O(epsilon). Dividing by epsilon and replacing r by the corrected radius costs only O(epsilon). The scalar averaged field is Lipschitz on the compact range; Gronwall gives an O(epsilon) error uniformly on the complete slow interval. Thus the growing observation time is covered, rather than justified by a formal pointwise average.

solutionSteps: x=r\cos\theta,\quad x\prime=-r\sin\theta,\quad r(0)=1,\quad\theta(0)=0.
r\prime=-\varepsilon r^{7}F(\theta),\quad F(\theta)=\cos^{6}\theta\sin^2\theta,
\theta\prime=1-\varepsilon r^{6}\cos^{7}\theta\sin\theta.
\textnormal{On slow times between zero and one, energy dissipation and the elementary differential inequality give }(1+6)^{-\frac{1}{6}}\le r\le1.
\overline F=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}F(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{(2m)!}{2\cdot4^m m!(m+1)!}\Bigg|_{m=3}=\frac{5}{128}.
\textnormal{Choose a bounded periodic primitive of the mean-zero part and correct the amplitude: }G\prime(\theta)=F(\theta)-\overline F,\quad\widetilde r=r+\varepsilon r^{7}G(\theta).

\textnormal{Direct differentiation cancels the oscillating drift. With slow time }\tau=\varepsilon t\textnormal{, the corrected variable satisfies uniformly }\frac{\mathrm d\widetilde r}{\mathrm d\tau}=-\frac{5}{128}\widetilde r^{7}+O(\varepsilon),\quad0\le\tau\le1.
\textnormal{Gronwall comparison gives uniform convergence to the averaged solution }R(\tau)=\left(1+\frac{15}{64}\tau\right)^{-\frac{1}{6}}.
\textnormal{Evaluate at slow time one.}

analyticCertificate: Almost surely both sinusoidal amplitudes are positive and unequal, so zero is a regular value on the periodic torus. For any regular level, the coarea formula for coordinate projections bounds total absolute horizontal variation by 4*pi*k and total absolute vertical variation by 4*pi; arclength is at most their sum. The bound is uniform in the level and coefficients. The band coarea average consequently converges to the zero-level length and is bounded by the same constant; the finite set of critical values has Lebesgue measure zero in the level parameter. Expectation and the limit can be interchanged by dominated convergence. At a fixed point all coefficient combinations are jointly Gaussian and have the explicitly checked diagonal covariance, hence are independent. Tonelli separates the spatial integral and expectation. Polar coordinates for two independent unit normals have independent uniform angle and Rayleigh radius with the checked mean. The angular integral reduces to the defined complete elliptic integral after a quarter-period shift. No external random-field formula is taken on trust.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At every fixed point, the field and its two partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian. Orthogonal coefficient vectors give }F\sim N(0,2),\quad F_x\sim N(0,1),\quad F_y\sim N(0,4),\textnormal{ independently; the second normal-distribution parameter is its variance.}

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }4\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(3).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+4Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+4\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+4\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{4}\pi E\left(\frac{3}{4}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}
4 \sqrt{2} \pi E\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At every fixed point, the field and its two partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian. Orthogonal coefficient vectors give }F\sim N(0,2),\quad F_x\sim N(0,1),\quad F_y\sim N(0,36),\textnormal{ independently; the second normal-distribution parameter is its variance.}

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }12\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(7).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+36Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+36\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+36\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{12}\pi E\left(\frac{35}{36}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}
12 \sqrt{2} \pi E\left(\frac{35}{36}\right)

analyticCertificate: Almost surely both sinusoidal amplitudes are positive and unequal, so zero is a regular value on the periodic torus. For any regular level, the coarea formula for coordinate projections bounds total absolute horizontal variation by 4*pi*k and total absolute vertical variation by 4*pi; arclength is at most their sum. The bound is uniform in the level and coefficients. The band coarea average consequently converges to the zero-level length and is bounded by the same constant; the finite set of critical values has Lebesgue measure zero in the level parameter. Expectation and the limit can be interchanged by dominated convergence. At a fixed point all coefficient combinations are jointly Gaussian and have the explicitly checked diagonal covariance, hence are independent. Tonelli separates the spatial integral and expectation. Polar coordinates for two independent unit normals have independent uniform angle and Rayleigh radius with the checked mean. The angular integral reduces to the defined complete elliptic integral after a quarter-period shift. No external random-field formula is taken on trust.

analyticCertificate: Almost surely both sinusoidal amplitudes are positive and unequal, so zero is a regular value on the periodic torus. For any regular level, the coarea formula for coordinate projections bounds total absolute horizontal variation by 4*pi*k and total absolute vertical variation by 4*pi; arclength is at most their sum. The bound is uniform in the level and coefficients. The band coarea average consequently converges to the zero-level length and is bounded by the same constant; the finite set of critical values has Lebesgue measure zero in the level parameter. Expectation and the limit can be interchanged by dominated convergence. At a fixed point all coefficient combinations are jointly Gaussian and have the explicitly checked diagonal covariance, hence are independent. Tonelli separates the spatial integral and expectation. Polar coordinates for two independent unit normals have independent uniform angle and Rayleigh radius with the checked mean. The angular integral reduces to the defined complete elliptic integral after a quarter-period shift. No external random-field formula is taken on trust.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At every fixed point, the field and its two partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian. Orthogonal coefficient vectors give }F\sim N(0,2),\quad F_x\sim N(0,1),\quad F_y\sim N(0,121),\textnormal{ independently; the second normal-distribution parameter is its variance.}

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }22\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(12).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+121Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+121\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+121\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{22}\pi E\left(\frac{120}{121}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}
22 \sqrt{2} \pi E\left(\frac{120}{121}\right)

statement: \textnormal{Let }A,B,C,D\textnormal{ be independent real standard-normal random variables, each with density }(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}.\textnormal{Let }\mathcal L\textnormal{ be the total Euclidean curve length of the zero set in the displayed square; counting or omitting the boundary does not affect this length almost surely. Find its expectation. The elliptic integral uses the displayed parameter convention.}\quad F(x,y)=A\cos x+B\sin x+C\cos(11y)+D\sin(11y),\quad(x,y)\in[0,2\pi]^2,\quad\mathcal L=\operatorname{Length}\{F=0\},\qquad E(p)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-p\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
